Issued at 200 PM CDT Sun Oct 25 2026

Near zonal flow is found over the northern Plains this 
afternoon in the wake of an exiting Hudson Bay low to our 
northeast, and a building negatively-tilted upper level ridge to
our west. Clear skies are expected to persist across the north 
this afternoon as surface high pressure bleeds in across the 
International Border, while cloud cover will persist across the 
south through the afternoon and overnight. Some isolated showers
will be possible over the south central this afternoon into 
this evening, mainly where the influx of mid level moisture 
meets a favorable area of ascent underneath the right entrance 
region of a departing H3 jet. Otherwise, mainly dry conditions 
are expected through this afternoon. Highs this afternoon are 
forecast from the mid 40s north to the lower 50s south, while 
winds turning anticyclonically around the high pressure center 
as it passes from west to east through the day. 

Late tonight into Monday, a closed low over the southeastern 
CONUS is progged to lift over the Rockies and into the northern 
Plains. Some initial chances for precpitation (30 to 60 percent)
will develop across the south ahead of this system as 
overrunning will promote increasing mid level saturation 
profiles, with the highest potential found across the southwest 
where better QG forcing is expected to develop overnight. Mainly
light rain is expected with this first round of precipitation 
overnight, though some light snow may begin to mix in during the
coolest period of early Monday morning. With near to 
subfreezing dewpt temps expected across much if not all of the 
forecast area overnight, lows are forecast from the upper teens 
to lower 20s north (where no cloud cover is anticipated), up to 
the mid 20s to lower 30s south (where thick cloud cover is 
expected to persist).

Higher chances for precpitation are then expected across 
portions of the forecast beginning Monday afternoon as the 
aforementioned upper level begins to lift across the Great 
Plains proper. Deterministic guidance has begun to advertise a 
much more diffuse, open wave passing over the North Dakota than 
previous forecast cycles due to the interference of another 
upper level low over the Pacific Northwest, Furthermore, model 
guidance has begun to deflect the surface low pressure system 
off the southeast as it contends with the presiding surface high
lingering over the southern Canadian Prairies through early 
next week, which may keep the axis of highest QPF displaced 
further to the south and east than earlier scenarios 
anticipated. Still, medium to high (60 to 90 percent) chances 
for precipitation are expected across much of southwestern and 
central North Dakota Monday afternoon through early Tuesday, 
with the highest chances across the southern James River Valley.
The main forecast challenge through this period is going to be 
the P-types. An interrogation of BUFKIT sounds reveals that the 
potential for snow across much of the forecast area is fairly 
limited, mainly as saturation throughout the DGZ is fairly 
transient. Some seeder-feeder effect over portions of the 
southwest into the south central may be sufficient to get at 
some moderate snowfall rates across this region, but locations 
elsewhere will likely struggle to overcome the still-warm ground
temperatures to see much more than a brief dusting of snow. 
Even where there's a decent chance for accumulating snowfall (30
to 60 percent across the southwest into south central as per 
the latest 5.2 NBM Calibrated Snowfall probability to exceed 
0.1" of snow), an initial round of low SLR snowfall would 
probably transition into more of a wintry mix through the early 
overnight period into Tuesday morning you lose ascent and 
saturation through the DGZ. Overall impacts from this event are 
expected to be limited at this time. 

Another round of precpitation is then possible across portions 
of the northwest and north central Tuesday afternoon through 
Wednesday morning as the aforementioned upper level low in the 
Pacific Northwest slides across Montana into the southern 
Canadian Prairies. The ensemble currently is advertising medium
to high chances (60 to 90 percent) for a mix of rain and snow 
as this low takes a more easterly track, though it remains 
fairly split between this scenario (55 percent of members), and 
one where a more westerly track will greatly limit our potential
for precipitation (45 percent). Neither scenario is expected to
promote any impacts across our area, with little to no QPF or 
snow accumulation expected. 

Behind this system, increasingly mild and dry conditions are 
anticipated through the remainder of the workweek. There's 
decent ensemble agreement on "warming" temperatures through this
period as a transient ridge builds downstream of another 
Pacific Low, promoting highs more broadly in the 50s and 
potentially the lower 60s by this coming weekend. Looking ahead
